world_status: statement found in an open source

earlier_scan.source_named: Wren, Lucy & Virginia Kemble 1994. Tagish Language Lessons (Yukon Native Language Centre); ynlc.ca connection refused.

new_statements.quote: The "tone" system of Tahgish comprises two levels, a low and a high, but I have the impression that there are likewise atonal syllables. In fact I have the impression that each word has a given tone level, either high or low, which applies to only the "full" syllables, all others being atonal. The atonal syllables seem to occur mostly before the tone, but once the tone level is set it continues through the rest of the word. Atonal syllables at the end of a word are always affixes. [...] Shuswap however has no tone but rather a weak stress on the first of the syllables with "full" vowel. Both these prosodic features need further investigation.
new_statements.citation: Marsh, Gordon H. 1959. Tentative Placing of the Tahgish Language within the Athapaskan Stock. Unpublished manuscript (revised from a paper read at the 1958 Annual Meeting of the Canadian Linguistic Association), sent with cover letter to Harry Hoijer, Vancouver, 11 Feb. 1959. Alaska Native Language Archive, Tagish language collection CN-TAGISH, folder 2.

new_statements.rule_in_words: No source states where word stress falls. Tagish is described as a tone language: two tone levels (high vs. low) on 'full' syllables, with reduced/atonal syllables (mostly prefixes before the tone-bearing part, and final affixes); each word is said to carry one tone level that persists to the end of the word. The 1994 practical orthography marks low tone with a grave accent (Tagish Literacy Workshop 1994: 5), i.e. a low-marked system, while the YNLC alphabet chart as summarised on Wikipedia marks high tone; neither says anything about stress.
new_statements.exceptions: Marsh flags his own record as sketchy (one elderly rememberer, 3 weeks in 1953) and says the prosodic features 'need further investigation'; his phoneme sheet adds 'length possibly prosodic (suprasegmental) rather than phonemic'.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level ('each word has a given tone level'), based on elicited citation forms and a comparative wordlist; no phrase-level statement.
new_statements.identity_note: Marsh 1959 data are from Patsy Henderson (Carcross, 1953), a rememberer who had not used the language for 40 years; Leer/Golla/McRoy/YNLC materials are from Angela Sidney and Lucy Wren (Carcross/Tagish). All are the same Tagish variety (tagi1240); Marsh's spelling 'Tahgish'. Tagish is sometimes treated as a dialect of a Tahltan-Kaska-Tagish complex (Tahltan tahl1239, Kaska kask1239).

sources.note: Ms. p. 6 (PDF p. 45): Tagish has a two-level tone system (low, high) plus 'atonal' syllables; each word carries one tone level that applies to its 'full' syllables and, once set, continues through the rest of the word; atonal syllables occur mostly before the tone and word-final atonal syllables are always affixes. Contrasts this with Shuswap, which 'has no tone but rather a weak stress'; no statement about a Tagish stress position. Data: 3 weeks in Aug. 1953 with one rememberer (Patsy Henderson, 75).

sources.citation: Wikipedia, 'Tagish language' (rev. 1345447973), Phonology > Tone section; and Tagish Alphabet chart (YNLC, via Wayback 2011).
sources.note: 'High tone is marked with (v́) on short vowels and (v́v) on long vowels while low tones remain unmarked' (cites the alphabet chart); 'Constricted vowels are pronounced with low tone' (cites Krauss & Golla 1981). Nothing on stress. The alphabet chart itself is a consonant/vowel table with no prose.

sources.note: 'Tagish sounds' section, p. 5 (PDF p. 8): 'The vowels are written with diacritics to indicate vowel length, nasalization, and low tone.... Low tone is indicated by a grave accent as in Southern Tutchone'; example p. 6 'low tone indicated by a grave accent over the vowel as in jìje berries'. No mention of stress.
